readerTitle: Your new hire learned your culture in a week. Not from the handbook.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑, 소프트웨어 스타트업) + 실제 연구 (Schein의 조직문화 3단계 모델)
insight: 문화는 벽에 붙은 가치가 아니라, 사람들이 무엇이 칭찬받고 무엇이 묵인되는지 보고 배운 행동 규칙이다.
misconception: 문화는 회사가 정해서 선언하는 가치, 복지, 사무실 분위기다. 좋은 가치 문구를 써 붙이면 문화가 생긴다.

sources.text: Schein, E. H. (1985). Organizational Culture and Leadership. Jossey-Bass. (artifacts, espoused values, basic underlying assumptions)
Deal, T. E. & Kennedy, A. A. (1982). Corporate Cultures. Addison-Wesley. ("the way we do things around here"라는 정의를 널리 알린 책)
레스토랑과 소프트웨어 스타트업 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Schein 모델의 세 층위 명칭(artifacts, espoused values, basic underlying assumptions)과 초판 연도(1985)를 게시 전 원서로 확인하세요. 카드에는 쉬운 말(what you can see / what people say / what people take for granted)로 풀어 썼습니다.
"the way we do things around here"는 Marvin Bower(McKinsey)에게서 나왔다는 설이 있고 Deal & Kennedy(1982)가 널리 알렸습니다. 출처가 불분명하므로 카드에서는 특정 인물에게 귀속하지 않고 'a common short definition'으로만 썼습니다.
"일주일 안에 문화를 배운다"는 연구 수치가 아니라 가상 사례 안의 설정입니다. 일반 주장으로 쓰지 않도록 hook 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: Your new hire learned your culture in a week. Not from the handbook.
body: Maya starts as a server at a busy bistro. A sign by the kitchen door reads: *Never rush a guest.*
By her second Friday, she is clearing plates before guests finish and dropping the bill with dessert. Nobody told her to. She worked it out by watching.

image.label: A server rushing past a kitchen sign that says Never rush a guest
image.brief: 따뜻한 조명의 비스트로 내부. 주방 문 옆에 "Never rush a guest" 손글씨 표지판. 그 앞을 접시를 든 신입 서버가 빠르게 지나가고, 테이블 손님은 아직 포크를 들고 있음. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You own the bistro. You want calmer, warmer service.
body: On Fridays, your manager loudly praises whoever turns tables fastest. Last week a guest waited 20 minutes for the bill and nobody followed up.
What would change how Maya serves guests the most?

options.text: Run a training session on the "never rush a guest" value
options.feedback: Training explains the rule, but on Friday Maya will still see speed get the praise. What she sees usually beats what she hears.

options.text: Change what gets praised on Friday, and follow up every time a guest is neglected
options.feedback: This changes the signals staff actually watch. It costs some speed on busy nights, and the manager has to change too.

options.text: Hire servers who are naturally warmer
options.feedback: Warm people help, but they adapt to what the shift rewards. Within weeks, many will rush like everyone else.

cards.title: Maya read three signals, not the sign.
body: In her first week, Maya noticed who got praised: the fastest server. She noticed what got ignored: the guest left waiting. And she noticed what the manager did when the rush hit: hurried everyone along.
None of this was written down. All of it was clear. The sign told her what the bistro *says*. The Friday shift told her what it *expects*.

image.label: Three signals: what gets praised, what gets ignored, what the boss does under pressure
image.brief: 아이콘 3개를 나란히 배치한 인포그래픽. 박수 아이콘 "What gets praised", 눈 감은 아이콘 "What gets ignored", 시계와 사람 아이콘 "What the boss does in a rush". 세 아이콘에서 화살표가 신입 서버 한 명에게 모임.

cards.title: Culture
body: **Culture** is the shared, mostly unspoken sense of what is expected here. It shows up in what people do when no rule tells them what to do.
A common short definition: *the way we do things around here.* Not the way we say we do things. The way we actually do them, especially when it's busy, hard or nobody's looking.
Every team has one, whether anyone designed it or not.

cards.title: Culture has layers, and the deepest one wins.
body: Organizational psychologist Edgar Schein described culture in three layers:
list: **What you can see:** decor, dress, posters, perks, how meetings run
**What people say:** stated values, mission, the handbook
**What people take for granted:** beliefs about what really gets you ahead or in trouble
cards.callout: When what people say clashes with what they take for granted, behavior follows the bottom layer.
cards.softwareNote: A beanbag room and a values page are the top two layers. Whether people admit a bug they shipped, or hide it, is the bottom one.

cards.title: Culture shows most in moments of tension.
body: Easy days reveal little. Culture shows when two goals collide: speed vs. care, a big customer vs. honesty, a star performer vs. a rule.

A warehouse says safety comes first, then praises the shift that skipped checks to hit a target. A hotel says guests come first, then blames the clerk who gave a refund. People remember who won those moments far longer than any speech.

cards.title: Don't read too much into one moment.
body: One rushed Friday doesn't define a culture. Patterns do: the same signal repeated across weeks and people.
And culture isn't simply good or bad. A fast, intense culture can suit a lunch counter and wreck a fine-dining room. The question is whether it fits what the business needs.
Finally, seeing your culture clearly is easier than changing it. That takes time, and it starts with the leader's own behavior.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: Your values page says: *We tell customers the truth.* A sales rep closes your biggest deal ever by promising a feature you haven't built. At the all-hands, the team cheers the win.

options.text: Celebrate the deal and quietly ask engineering to build the feature fast
options.feedback: You keep the revenue and the mood. But everyone just learned that stretching the truth gets applause.

options.text: Keep the deal, tell the customer the real timeline, and say openly why at the next all-hands
options.feedback: It may cost an awkward call or the deal itself. But the team sees honesty win a real moment, which teaches more than any page.

options.text: Send a company-wide email reminding everyone of the honesty value
options.feedback: It states the value again, but the cheering stays unanswered. People weigh what happened over what was written.

cards.title: Culture is what people learn is rewarded and tolerated.
body: Your team reads your culture from what you praise, what you let slide and what you do under pressure. The poster is the smallest part.
**Try it today:** write down the last three things you praised and one thing you let pass. What would a new hire conclude from that list alone?
